lawyer:
M Shamsul Alam, Deputy Attorney-General, instructed by Zinnur Ahmed, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant. 
Serajul Huq, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
State ----- Appellant.
Vs.
MM Rafiqul Hyder ----- Accused-Respondent.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J.: I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Afzal, J. I agree that acquittal of the respondent by the Appellate Court is highly improper and that this appeal by the State should be allowed. I, however, like to add a few words in connection with the respondent's contention that the trial was vitiated by mis-joinder of charges and want of jurisdiction of the Tribunal in trying a schedule offence along with a non-schedule offence. 

 2. This question has been elaborately discussed by my learned brother in his judgment. What I find is that it is neither a case of mis-joinder of charges nor a case of trial without jurisdiction. The offence allegedly committed by the respondent is the offence of smuggling of gold into Bangladesh. Smuggling particularly of gold has been defined in the Special Powers Act and this definition is exactly the same as that of smuggling under section 156(8) of the Customs Act. The offence is one and same. Therefore there is no question of joinder or mis-joinder of charges. Though it has been made punishable under both the laws, but to try this offence exclusive jurisdiction has been given only to the Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, and as such, jurisdiction of an ordinary court, such as a Magistrate to try the offence under ordinary law stands ousted. The respondent was rightly charged by the Tribunal under section 25B of the said Act and after trial he was rightly convicted under section 25B of the Act. The addition of the words "read with section 156(8)" in the charge is superfluous and totally unnecessary. This addition has not affected the Tribunal's jurisdiction to try the offence. 

 16. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division rightly rejected the prosecution evidence as to the recovery of the gold from the possession of the respondent, particularly the evidence of the customs officers, PWs 1 and 2; and the own statement of the respondent (Ext. 2) causing no failure of justice and whether it was also rightly held that the trial was vitiated by the joinder of the scheduled and non-scheduled offences. 

 17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the State submitted that the recovery of the gold from the disputed Echolac handbag being admitted, the unimpeachable evidence adduced by the prosecution, both oral and documentary, showing clearly that the said bag belonged to the respondent was illegally rejected by the High Court Division on untenable grounds causing a manifest failure of justice. He also submitted that the appellate court in acquitting the respondent neither gave any consideration to the gravely incriminating facts and circumstances relied upon by the trial Court nor properly weighed the observations made by the trial court with regard to the demeanour and quality of the evidence of the witnesses from the Biman. PWs 5-7 and thus acted contrary to the rules and practices of the appellate Court He further submitted that upon a wrong view of the law and the facts of the present case it was erroneously held that the joinder of the scheduled and non-scheduled offences vitiated the entire proceeding. 

 19. To take up the last point rust, the High Court Division held that the Special Tribunal acted illegally in taking cognizance of the offence under section 156(8) of the Customs Act which is a non-scheduled offence and trying the same with the scheduled offence under section 25B (1) of the Special Powers Act and such joinder of non-scheduled and scheduled offence in the same trial vitiated the entire proceeding. Reliance in this connection was placed on two decisions, 33 DLR 203 (Tamiz Mia vs. Bangladesh) and 3S DLR 127 (Talukder A Aziz vs. State). 

 20. It is to be observed that it is absolutely correct to say that a Special Tribunal constituted under the Act has been vested with the jurisdiction to try the offences specified in the schedule to the said Act and no other offence although the Tribunal Judge is the same person as the Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge, etc. A special Tribunal should, therefore, be careful taking cognizance under the Act so that it does not take Cognizance of and proceed to trial of any offence which is not included in the schedule. Under the CrPC if the acts alleged constitute an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law the person accused of them may be charged with and tried at one trial for each of such offences unlike under the Act under which only the offences mentioned in the schedule may be tried by a Special Tribunal and no other. If, however, through inadvertence a non-scheduled offence is included in the trial of a scheduled offence the trial does not necessarily become void or without jurisdiction entirely but a question may be raised as to whether the accused was prejudiced by such joinder and in a particular case there may be necessity to set aside such a trial and direct a trial afresh. We do not think that this aspect has been sufficiently considered by the High Court Division either in the present case or in the two other cases which were relied upon. However, it will be seen that the facts of the said two cases were materially different from the facts of the present case and whatever has been decided in these cases cannot be cited in the facts of the present case. In those cases the proceedings under the Act were also in respect of offences under the Penal Code which are not included in the schedule. The entire proceedings have been held to be void and without jurisdiction without considering that so far as the scheduled offence was concerned there was no lack of jurisdiction and no good reason has been given for holding that the entire proceeding became void and without jurisdiction for including Penal Code offences. For, the present, we are distinguishing those cases on facts in that in the present case although section 156(8) of the Customs Act has been referred to, which is a non-scheduled offence, the fact remains that the offence, alleged in the case for which the trial was held was one and, the Same i.e. smuggling of gold. The offence of smuggling of gold as defined in section 15B of the Act is exactly the same as in the Customs Act. 

 21. Mr. Serajul Huq has not disputed this proposition. He has, however, submitted that if it were any other goods it would be possible to contend that the definition of smuggling under the two Acts is different since we are dealing with gold in the present case we need not examine Mi. Huq's contention as to other goods. The facts alleged in the present case attract the definition of 'smuggling of gold under both the Acts. If that be so, and it is so, then it cannot be doubted that the Special Tribunal under the Act has exclusive jurisdiction by reason of section 26 of the Act to try such an offence of smuggling. All other courts are excluded to take cognizance of the offence of smuggling of gold and it makes no difference in mentioning section 156(8) of the Customs, Act while framing a charge for smuggling of gold under the Act because no other court will have jurisdiction to try such an offence. The charge under section 156(8) of the Customs Act in the facts of 'the present case was a mere surplusage and in such view of the matter we are clearly of the opinion that the High Court Division wrongly held that the entire proceeding was vitiated by the joinder of the scheduled and non-scheduled offences. 

 25. There is a good deal of force in the submission of the learned Deputy Attorney-General. It is clear from Ext. 2 that the respondent did not admit that he had brought the gold concealing it inside the bag. He only claimed ownership of the bag but not of the gold. It is evident; therefore, that the statement could not be regarded as a confession because the law is now well settled that it is only when the statement of the accused can be read as a plenary admission of guilt in straight and clear terms that it can be taken as a confession of the crime. All confessions are admissions but not vice-versa. From a plain reading of Ext. 2 it appears that it was admissible as an admission but not as a confession as there was no plenary admission of guilt by the respondent Section 24 of the Evidence Act makes a confession irrelevant in a criminal proceeding if it appears to have been caused by inducement, threat or promise proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient in the opinion of the court to give the accused person grounds which would appear to him reasonable for supposing that by making it he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil of a temporal nature in reference to the proceedings against him. Not being a confession the invocation of section 24 of the Evidence Act was wholly irrelevant for excluding Ext. 2 and the learned Judges misdirected themselves in holding that the statement was barred under the said section. Mr. Serajul Huq readily agreed now that section 24 was wrongly applied in the facts of the case but it is he who, it appears, made the argument in the High Court Division relying on section 24. Mr. Huq argued before us that the High Court Division also rejected Ext. 2 on the basis of the evidence of PW 5 that it was written on the dictation of a customs official. We shall consider the treatment of the evidence of the Biman witnesses separately as made by the trial Court and the High Court Division. For the present it is sufficient to observe that the trial Court upon giving better reasons rejected the evidence of PW 5 and relied upon the written statement of the respondent, Ext. 2. We shall only add that the defence contention that the said statement (Ext. 2) was forcibly obtained. (about which there is no evidence) by the customs officers is rather inconsistent with the obliging evidence of PW5 in cross-examination that he found the respondent writing the statement on the dictation of a Customs Officer. It was also an obvious improvement in his examination-in-chief where he merely stated that he found the respondent writing a statement. Further there is nothing on record to show that the respondent had made any complaint to anybody that the customs officers had forced threatened or coerced him in any manner to write the statement as dictated by them. The respondent was not an ordinary, uninitiated traveller but a member of a sophisticated service in International Flights of the Bangladesh Biman. It was easy for him to reach any superior officer of the Biman or the Civil Aviation Authority at ZIA and make a complaint at once if there was any truth in the allegation that the customs officials were trying to frame him in a false case of smuggling. Mr. Serajul Huq felt the difficulty in advancing any argument as to alleged pressure and coercion by the customs officers but submitted. perhaps as a last resort, that the respondent might have made the statement having been given some kind of assurance by the customs officers as he must have become nonplussed having found himself pitted against a grave charge of smuggling of gold, We have not the slightest hesitation in rejecting the submission of Mr. Huq which has no basis and we hold that the High Court Division was clearly wrong in rejecting Ext, 2 as inadmissible and unreliable. In our opinion Ext. 2 is both admissible and reliable and is sufficient to establish the prosecution case that the disputed handbag belonged to the respondent 

 27. It is well-settled that where a finding of fact is based upon the credibility of evidence involving the appreciation of the demeanour of witnesses the view of the trial Court is entitled to great weight and should not be lightly discarded. We do not think that the High Court Division in the present case discarded the view of the trial Court with reasonable justification. It has been observed that the trial Court did not record anything suspicious in their evidence or attitude at the time of recording evidence and did not suggest to these witnesses that they were making untrue statements to oblige the defence and while writing the judgment after more than a month whimsically and abruptly said without giving cogent and convincing reason that they were concealing something for helping the appellant. Before finding fault with the trial Court and proceeding to rely on the truthfulness of PWs 5-7, the learned Judges should have noticed the solid reasons given by the trial Court in believing that the disputed handbag belonged to the respondent. Much has been made out of the evidence of PWs 6 and 7 in cross-examination to the effect that the respondent had told the customs officers at the counter that the bag did not belong to him and that the crew baggages bear tags (which was neither seized from nor seen with the disputed bag at the time of trial). It has been observed that none of the witnesses, PW s 5-7, was declared hostile by the Prosecution and so their evidence cannot be discarded only because they are favourable to the respondent. It has also been observed that the seizure list does not show any seizure of tags which could prove beyond doubt that the bag belonged to the respondent. 

 30. The High Court Division not only completely ignored this vital aspect of the evidence, but went on to depict the customs officers (PWs 1 and 2) testimony as unreliable. Why? Has the defence been able to shake their evidence in any way? Any motive for false implication in a got up case involving 310 toles of gold? None. Only a vague suggestion was given to PW 1 that the respondent was falsely implicated because he refused to oblige them by bringing ‘এটি সেটি’ as requested by them from time to time. The High Court Division failed to notice that their evidence is completely in accord with the contemporaneous documents, i.e. Exts.1 and 2 and the surrounding circumstances. We have already said that there is nothing on record to show that the respondent an air-crew of the Biman, who had just landed from Dubai made any attempt to reach any of the authorities either of the Biman or of the Airport to make any complaint while he was allegedly being grilled by the customs officers falsely on a serious charge. The events rather show that he meekly submitted to the search and seizure which is consistent with the conduct only of a guilty person. 

 31. It appears that the High Court Division misread the evidence of PW 1 and upon such misreading held him to be unreliable. That he was present at the time of recovery of the gold in the room of the Deputy Collector is borne out by his signature in Ext. 1. His presence is not also disputed. What he said in cross-examination was that he was not present at the time of the examination of the baggage of the respondent. In the context of the statement the reference was to the examination at the counter. There is no inconsistency with his deposition in chief. It is quite possible that he saw the respondent himself placing his baggage’s for checking before another Inspector but might not have been present at the time of actual examination. The High Court Division was plainly wrong in thinking that the witness contradicted himself or that he was trying to save another person to whom the bag belonged which 'was nobody's case. The main reason for disbelieving PWs 1 and 2 seems to be that the tag of the handbag was not seized. It is not understood what has been meant by the observation that the non-seizure of the baggage tag along with the Echolac bag was a deliberate act on the part of the Customs Officer for keeping a gap in the continuity of events and that has been done with intention. The learned Judges lost sight of the broad fact that there was no-valid reason for thinking that the customs officers falsely implicated the respondent in a pre-planned manner out of any motive as suggested by the defence. They were doing their official duty in a routine manner. PWs 1 and 2 stated that the respondent himself placed his baggages at the crew baggage examination counter. Unless he pointed out his baggages himself there would not have been any occasion to start' the examination. So the identification of the baggages being already there, the non-seizure of the tag, in our opinion, cannot be held to be fatal for the prosecution. Moreover, the subsequent evidence of acknowledgement of the handbag by the respondent from which the gold was recovered made the issue of non-seizure of tag wholly immaterial. 

 33. Similarly the learned Judges wrongly relied upon the evidence of PWs 6 and 7 that the respondent had told the customs officers at the counter that the bag did not belong to him. The obliging nature of their evidence is apparent because it is none of the business of a customs officer to make an inquiry as to any baggage which may be lying for examination. It is the duty of the passenger or crew to identify his or her baggage for examination. If a particular baggage is not identified by anybody, it remains as an unclaimed baggage. The respondent's plea that his handbag was missing and at that time PW 2 pointed out the particular bag and in spite of his disowning the same, he was attributed with the ownership thereof, can only be accepted if he had been able to show that PW 2 had any motive or design to implicate him falsely in a serious case like this. Strangely enough, there is no such suggestion even to PW 2. 

 36. None of the findings made by the learned Judges including the main finding that the prosecution failed to prove that the Echolac bag (in which the gold bars have been found) actually belonged to the respondent or was identified at the Customs Counter or at any stage by the respondent appears to be justified in view of the law and the facts and circumstances proved in the case.
